claim: The cryoEM structure of PepMV was determined at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: We present the cryoEM structure of PepMV virions at 3.9 Å of resolution.
evidence: The resolution is stated directly in the text and supported by FSC analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PepMV has a left-handed helical structure with a diameter of 130 Å.
source: The cryoEM map reveals a left-handed helix with a diameter of 130 Å and an inner narrow channel of 13 Å, and the structure shows a pitch of 34.6 Å and 8.7 CP copies per turn.
evidence: Direct measurement from the cryoEM map as described in the Results section.

claim: PepMV has an inner narrow channel of 13 Å.
source: The cryoEM map reveals a left-handed helix with a diameter of 130 Å and an inner narrow channel of 13 Å, and the structure shows a pitch of 34.6 Å and 8.7 CP copies per turn.
evidence: Direct measurement from the cryoEM map.

claim: PepMV has a helical pitch of 34.6 Å.
source: The cryoEM map reveals a left-handed helix with a diameter of 130 Å and an inner narrow channel of 13 Å, and the structure shows a pitch of 34.6 Å and 8.7 CP copies per turn.
evidence: Direct measurement from the cryoEM map.

claim: PepMV has 8.7 CP copies per helical turn.
source: The cryoEM map reveals a left-handed helix with a diameter of 130 Å and an inner narrow channel of 13 Å, and the structure shows a pitch of 34.6 Å and 8.7 CP copies per turn.
evidence: Direct measurement from the cryoEM map and helical symmetry determination.

claim: The PepMV cryoEM structure represents the highest resolution structural data for a flexible filamentous virion to date.
source: Our cryoEM map reaches near-atomic resolution, to date the highest resolution structural data for a flexible filamentous virion, where bulky protein side chains are discernible (Figure 1C).
evidence: Comparison with previously published structures of flexible filamentous viruses.

claim: Bulky protein side chains are discernible in the PepMV cryoEM map.
source: Our cryoEM map reaches near-atomic resolution, to date the highest resolution structural data for a flexible filamentous virion, where bulky protein side chains are discernible (Figure 1C).
evidence: Visual inspection of the cryoEM map shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PepMV CP has an all-helix fold.
source: The modeled structure for PepMV CP is, as defined for PapMV CP, an all-helix fold, and the low RMSD between the two structures (1.5 Å in the core region) reflects their clear homology (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Atomic model built from the cryoEM map.

claim: The RMSD between PepMV CP and PapMV CP core regions is 1.5 Å.
source: The modeled structure for PepMV CP is, as defined for PapMV CP, an all-helix fold, and the low RMSD between the two structures (1.5 Å in the core region) reflects their clear homology (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Structural comparison calculation between the two atomic models.

claim: PepMV CP has three major regions: the core, an N-terminal flexible arm, and a C-terminal extension.
source: The PepMV CP structure thus generated has three major regions: the core; an N-terminal flexible arm; and a C-terminal extension.
evidence: Structural analysis of the atomic model.

claim: The first 20 amino acids in the N-terminal side of PepMV CP are not included in the atomic model due to high flexibility.
source: The first 20 amino acids in the N-terminal side are not included in the atomic model because the region projects outwards, and its density vanishes due to high flexibility.
evidence: Lack of visible density in the cryoEM map for this region.

claim: Each PepMV CP binds five ribonucleotides.
source: Each CP binds five ribonucleotides (Figure 1D), so that the entire genome of PepMV would require 1290 copies of PepMV CP spanning 510 nm (3.95 Å of axial rise/subunit), which agrees with the 509 nm length originally reported for the virus (Jones et al., 1980).
evidence: Analysis of the cryoEM map showing RNA density associated with each CP subunit.

claim: The entire PepMV genome requires 1290 copies of PepMV CP.
source: Each CP binds five ribonucleotides (Figure 1D), so that the entire genome of PepMV would require 1290 copies of PepMV CP spanning 510 nm (3.95 Å of axial rise/subunit), which agrees with the 509 nm length originally reported for the virus (Jones et al., 1980).
evidence: Calculation based on genome size and number of nucleotides per CP.

claim: The calculated length of PepMV virion is 510 nm.
source: Each CP binds five ribonucleotides (Figure 1D), so that the entire genome of PepMV would require 1290 copies of PepMV CP spanning 510 nm (3.95 Å of axial rise/subunit), which agrees with the 509 nm length originally reported for the virus (Jones et al., 1980).
evidence: Calculation based on number of CP copies and axial rise per subunit.

claim: The calculated PepMV virion length agrees with the originally reported length of 509 nm.
source: Each CP binds five ribonucleotides (Figure 1D), so that the entire genome of PepMV would require 1290 copies of PepMV CP spanning 510 nm (3.95 Å of axial rise/subunit), which agrees with the 509 nm length originally reported for the virus (Jones et al., 1980).
evidence: Comparison with previously published measurement.

claim: The ssRNA in PepMV runs in a helix of 70 Å in diameter.
source: The ssRNA runs in a helix of 70 Å in diameter (Figure 1B).
evidence: Measurement from the cryoEM map.

claim: Individual nucleotides are clearly separated in the cryoEM map.
source: The signal clearly separates the individual nucleotides, but we could not identify the bases due to the helical averaging of the variable sequence of the ssRNA.
evidence: Visual inspection of the cryoEM density for RNA.

claim: The bases of individual nucleotides could not be identified due to helical averaging of the variable RNA sequence.
source: The signal clearly separates the individual nucleotides, but we could not identify the bases due to the helical averaging of the variable sequence of the ssRNA.
evidence: Limitation of helical reconstruction method when applied to non-uniform sequences.

claim: The ssRNA resides in a continuous groove with high electropositive potential.
source: The results show that the RNA resides in a continuous groove with a high electropositive potential (Figure 2A) constructed by CPs from consecutive turns of the helix.
evidence: Electrostatic potential calculation from the atomic model.

claim: The RNA-binding groove is constructed by CPs from consecutive turns of the helix.
source: The results show that the RNA resides in a continuous groove with a high electropositive potential (Figure 2A) constructed by CPs from consecutive turns of the helix.
evidence: Structural analysis of CP arrangement in the virion.

claim: S92 and S94 might interact with the phosphate backbone of ssRNA at positions 1 and 3.
source: Several amino acids display potential interactions with the phosphate backbone of the ssRNA. S92 and S94 in one face, and Q203 at the opposite side of the ssRNA might interact at positions 1 and 3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: MDFF simulation and structural analysis.

claim: Q203 might interact with the phosphate backbone of ssRNA at positions 1 and 3.
source: Several amino acids display potential interactions with the phosphate backbone of the ssRNA. S92 and S94 in one face, and Q203 at the opposite side of the ssRNA might interact at positions 1 and 3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: MDFF simulation and structural analysis.

claim: R124, D163, and K196 might establish H-bonding contacts with the RNA base at position 2.
source: Three polar-charged residues, R124, D163, and K196 might establish H-bonding contacts with this RNA base.
evidence: MDFF simulation and structural analysis of protein-RNA interactions.

claim: D163 is in the most conserved region within the genus Potexvirus.
source: D163 is in the most conserved region within the genus Potexvirus, and the consensus sequence FDFFD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) constructs the floor of the RNA binding pocket.
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The consensus sequence FDFFD constructs the floor of the RNA binding pocket.
source: D163 is in the most conserved region within the genus Potexvirus, and the consensus sequence FDFFD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) constructs the floor of the RNA binding pocket.
evidence: Structural analysis of the RNA-binding site.

claim: The RNA binding pocket is large enough to accommodate pyrimidines or purines.
source: This pocket is large enough to accommodate pyrimidines or purines, and the presence of three amino acids ensures the interaction with the RNA regardless of the nucleotide.
evidence: Structural analysis of pocket dimensions.

claim: Three amino acids in the binding pocket ensure interaction with RNA regardless of the nucleotide type.
source: This pocket is large enough to accommodate pyrimidines or purines, and the presence of three amino acids ensures the interaction with the RNA regardless of the nucleotide.
evidence: Structural analysis and inference about binding specificity.

claim: R124, D163, and K196 are required for cell-to-cell movement of PepMV.
source: The results (Figure 2E) reveal that the three amino acids at the binding pocket for nucleotide at position 2 (R124, D163 and K196) are required to complement the cell-to-cell movement of the CP-defective PepMV mutant, suggesting a disruption of the CP-RNA interaction needed in virus intercellular transport.
evidence: Trans-complementation assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations in R124, D163, and K196 disrupt CP-RNA interaction needed for virus intercellular transport.
source: The results (Figure 2E) reveal that the three amino acids at the binding pocket for nucleotide at position 2 (R124, D163 and K196) are required to complement the cell-to-cell movement of the CP-defective PepMV mutant, suggesting a disruption of the CP-RNA interaction needed in virus intercellular transport.
evidence: Inference from trans-complementation assay results.

claim: Mutant K93A impairs viral propagation within the inoculated leaf.
source: Mutant K93A also impairs viral propagation within the inoculated leaf, probably due to structural changes at the loop that contains S92 and S94.
evidence: Trans-complementation assay results.

claim: K93A mutation probably causes structural changes at the loop containing S92 and S94.
source: Mutant K93A also impairs viral propagation within the inoculated leaf, probably due to structural changes at the loop that contains S92 and S94.
evidence: Inference based on structural proximity and functional assay results.

claim: Q203A mutant shows reduced movement between cells but not full impairment.
source: In the case of mutant Q203A, it seems that there is a reduced movement between cells but not full impairment.
evidence: Trans-complementation assay results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Only wild-type and Q203A mutant produced fully assembled virions.
source: Attempts to purify PepMV virions were only fruitful for the wt and for the Q203A mutant (Figure 2F), suggesting the lack of full viral assembly in the rest of PepMV CP mutants.
evidence: Western blot analysis of virion preparations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Single amino acid changes in CP can impair CP-RNA binding.
source: Single amino acid changes appear to impair CP-RNA binding, probably including a cooperative effect between the hundreds of CP copies that build the virions.
evidence: Inference from mutagenesis and virion assembly experiments.

claim: There is a cooperative effect between the hundreds of CP copies that build the virions.
source: Single amino acid changes appear to impair CP-RNA binding, probably including a cooperative effect between the hundreds of CP copies that build the virions.
evidence: Inference from the observation that single mutations prevent virion assembly.

claim: The helical assembly of PepMV is mediated by the CP N-terminal arm and C-terminal extension.
source: As described for BaMV (DiMaio et al., 2015), the helical assembly of PepMV is mediated by the CP N-terminal arm and C-terminal extension.
evidence: Structural analysis and comparison with BaMV.

claim: The N-terminal arm from the Ni subunit interacts with a hydrophobic groove of the Ni-1 subunit.
source: The N-terminal arm from the Ni subunit interacts with a hydrophobic groove of the Ni-1 subunit and establishes the main side-by-side contact in the helical arrangement (Figures 1A and 3A).
evidence: Structural analysis of CP-CP interactions in the cryoEM map.

claim: The N-terminal arm establishes the main side-by-side contact in the helical arrangement.
source: The N-terminal arm from the Ni subunit interacts with a hydrophobic groove of the Ni-1 subunit and establishes the main side-by-side contact in the helical arrangement (Figures 1A and 3A).
evidence: Structural analysis of the helical assembly.

claim: F28 from Ni fits into a hydrophobic pocket in Ni-1.
source: A hydrophobic pocket in Ni-1 accommodates part of the N-terminal arm, where F28 from Ni fits (Figure 3B).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A similar type of interaction via F13 was observed in the crystal structure of PapMV CP.
source: A similar type of interaction was observed between subunits in the crystal structure of PapMV CP via amino acid F13 (Yang et al., 2012), and for BaMV, by residue W41 (DiMaio et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with published crystal structure.

claim: BaMV uses residue W41 for a similar type of subunit interaction.
source: A similar type of interaction was observed between subunits in the crystal structure of PapMV CP via amino acid F13 (Yang et al., 2012), and for BaMV, by residue W41 (DiMaio et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with published BaMV structure.

claim: F28A mutant allows cell-to-cell movement but does not produce fully assembled virions.
source: The F28 mutant allows cell-to-cell movement (Figure 3C) but does not produce fully assembled virions (Figure 3D), suggesting that the tested mutation allows for the functional separation of the cell-to-cell movement of PepMV from the encapsidation of fully assembled virions, reinforcing the notion of a non-virion RNP structure during the intercellular movement of potexviruses through plasmodesmata (Lough et al., 2000).
evidence: Trans-complementation and virion purification assays shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: F28A mutation allows functional separation of cell-to-cell movement from encapsidation of fully assembled virions.
source: The F28 mutant allows cell-to-cell movement (Figure 3C) but does not produce fully assembled virions (Figure 3D), suggesting that the tested mutation allows for the functional separation of the cell-to-cell movement of PepMV from the encapsidation of fully assembled virions, reinforcing the notion of a non-virion RNP structure during the intercellular movement of potexviruses through plasmodesmata (Lough et al., 2000).
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: Potexviruses use a non-virion RNP structure during intercellular movement through plasmodesmata.
source: The F28 mutant allows cell-to-cell movement (Figure 3C) but does not produce fully assembled virions (Figure 3D), suggesting that the tested mutation allows for the functional separation of the cell-to-cell movement of PepMV from the encapsidation of fully assembled virions, reinforcing the notion of a non-virion RNP structure during the intercellular movement of potexviruses through plasmodesmata (Lough et al., 2000).
evidence: Inference from current results combined with previous literature.

claim: The C-terminal extension builds the inner wall of the virus.
source: On the other hand, the C-terminal extension, a long coil with a short α-helix in its last part, builds the inner wall of the virus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Structural analysis of the cryoEM map.

claim: The C-terminal extension is a long coil with a short α-helix in its last part.
source: On the other hand, the C-terminal extension, a long coil with a short α-helix in its last part, builds the inner wall of the virus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Structural analysis of the atomic model.

claim: The C-terminal segment runs along the axial channel and creates a network of small and local interactions.
source: This C-terminal segment describes a turn that runs along the axial channel and creates a network of small and local interactions (Figure 3E), where each subunit contacts neighbours at upper and lower levels.
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Each C-terminal extension contacts neighbors at upper and lower levels.
source: This C-terminal segment describes a turn that runs along the axial channel and creates a network of small and local interactions (Figure 3E), where each subunit contacts neighbours at upper and lower levels.
evidence: Structural analysis of inter-subunit contacts.

claim: The C-terminal extensions are responsible for axial interactions that support helix formation.
source: Thus, the C-terminal extensions are responsible for the axial interactions that support helix formation.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis of C-terminal interactions.

claim: Flexible links between PepMV CPs via N-terminal arm and C-terminal region allow for relative movements between CPs.
source: As for BaMV (DiMaio et al., 2015), the flexible links between PepMV CPs via N-terminal arm and C-terminal region allow for relative movements between CPs and explain the flexuous nature of the virions.
evidence: Structural analysis and comparison with BaMV.

claim: Flexible links between CPs explain the flexuous nature of the virions.
source: As for BaMV (DiMaio et al., 2015), the flexible links between PepMV CPs via N-terminal arm and C-terminal region allow for relative movements between CPs and explain the flexuous nature of the virions.
evidence: Inference from structural features.

claim: The CP structure from potexviruses shares its topology with the NP of several representatives of genus Phlebovirus.
source: The search revealed that the CP structure from potexviruses shares its topology with the NP of several representatives of genus Phlebovirus (family Bunyaviridae), such as Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), Toscana virus, and Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV).
evidence: Dali server search for structural homologs.

claim: Potexvirus CP shares topology with NP from RVFV, Toscana virus, and SFTSV.
source: The search revealed that the CP structure from potexviruses shares its topology with the NP of several representatives of genus Phlebovirus (family Bunyaviridae), such as Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), Toscana virus, and Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV).
evidence: Dali server structural comparison results.

claim: Genera Potexvirus and Phlebovirus belong to different superfamilies of RNA viruses based on RdRp phylogeny.
source: Genera Potexvirus and Phlebovirus belong to different superfamilies of RNA viruses when these are classified based on phylogenetic relationships among RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) and also have different genomic organizations (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to established viral classification.

claim: Potexvirus and Phlebovirus have different genomic organizations.
source: Genera Potexvirus and Phlebovirus belong to different superfamilies of RNA viruses when these are classified based on phylogenetic relationships among RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) and also have different genomic organizations (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to established viral classification.

claim: Phleboviruses have segmented (-)ssRNA associated with NP in loose RNPs.
source: They have segmented (-)ssRNA associated with the NP in loose RNPs (Raymond et al., 2012), and these are protected inside an icosahedral shell of glycoproteins inserted in a membrane, as has been observed for RVFV (Huiskonen et al., 2009, Freiberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to published phlebovirus structures.

claim: Phlebovirus RNPs are protected inside an icosahedral shell of glycoproteins inserted in a membrane.
source: They have segmented (-)ssRNA associated with the NP in loose RNPs (Raymond et al., 2012), and these are protected inside an icosahedral shell of glycoproteins inserted in a membrane, as has been observed for RVFV (Huiskonen et al., 2009, Freiberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to published RVFV structures.

claim: Potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP have a TM-score of 0.51 when aligned.
source: The topology of CP from potexviruses and of the NP from phleboviruses (illustrated for RVFV) are, nonetheless, very similar (Figures 4A and 4C) and show a TM-score of 0.51 when aligned, pointing to a common family fold (Zhang and Skolnick, 2005).
evidence: TM-score calculation from structural alignment.

claim: A TM-score of 0.51 points to a common family fold between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP.
source: The topology of CP from potexviruses and of the NP from phleboviruses (illustrated for RVFV) are, nonetheless, very similar (Figures 4A and 4C) and show a TM-score of 0.51 when aligned, pointing to a common family fold (Zhang and Skolnick, 2005).
evidence: Interpretation of TM-score based on established criteria.

claim: Similarities between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP include the overall topology of the all-alpha helical domain.
source: The similarities include: the overall topology of the all-alpha helical domain; the N-terminal arm and its binding site from the adjacent protomer, and hence, the side-by-side mechanism for oligomerization; the groove for the ssRNA binding; and the relative positions of all these elements.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: Similarities between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP include the N-terminal arm and its binding site from the adjacent protomer.
source: The similarities include: the overall topology of the all-alpha helical domain; the N-terminal arm and its binding site from the adjacent protomer, and hence, the side-by-side mechanism for oligomerization; the groove for the ssRNA binding; and the relative positions of all these elements.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: Potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP share a side-by-side mechanism for oligomerization.
source: The similarities include: the overall topology of the all-alpha helical domain; the N-terminal arm and its binding site from the adjacent protomer, and hence, the side-by-side mechanism for oligomerization; the groove for the ssRNA binding; and the relative positions of all these elements.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: Similarities between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP include the groove for ssRNA binding.
source: The similarities include: the overall topology of the all-alpha helical domain; the N-terminal arm and its binding site from the adjacent protomer, and hence, the side-by-side mechanism for oligomerization; the groove for the ssRNA binding; and the relative positions of all these elements.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: Phlebovirus NPs have been observed in tetrameric, pentameric, and hexameric oligomers.
source: The crystallographic studies with phlebovirus NPs have shown tetrameric, pentameric, and hexameric oligomers, in which each NP interacts with the core of the adjacent subunit via an N-terminal arm (Zhou et al., 2013) following the same side-by-side polymerization mechanism shown in potexviruses.
evidence: Reference to crystallographic studies.

claim: In phlebovirus NP oligomers, each NP interacts with the core of the adjacent subunit via an N-terminal arm.
source: The crystallographic studies with phlebovirus NPs have shown tetrameric, pentameric, and hexameric oligomers, in which each NP interacts with the core of the adjacent subunit via an N-terminal arm (Zhou et al., 2013) following the same side-by-side polymerization mechanism shown in potexviruses.
evidence: Reference to crystallographic studies.

claim: The divergence between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP is in their C-terminal regions.
source: The divergence between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP is in their C-terminal regions.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: The C-terminus in PepMV CP protrudes from the core domain and allows longitudinal interactions for helix building.
source: The C-terminus in PepMV CP protrudes from the core domain (Figure 4B) and allows longitudinal interactions for helix building.
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The C-terminus of phlebovirus NP folds back into the core region and participates in the RNA-binding site.
source: The C-terminus of the phlebovirus NP folds back into the core region and participates in the RNA-binding site that incorporates seven bases/subunit (Figure 4D).
evidence: Structural analysis of phlebovirus NP structure.

claim: Phlebovirus NP incorporates seven bases per subunit.
source: The C-terminus of the phlebovirus NP folds back into the core region and participates in the RNA-binding site that incorporates seven bases/subunit (Figure 4D).
evidence: Reference to phlebovirus NP structure.

claim: The location of the C-terminal arm in phlebovirus NPs cannot support longitudinal assembly.
source: The location of the C-terminal arm in phlebovirus NPs cannot support a longitudinal assembly, and hence, their RNPs remain more loosely associated (Raymond et al., 2012) than in their plant-virus counterparts.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis.

claim: Phlebovirus RNPs remain more loosely associated than potexvirus virions.
source: The location of the C-terminal arm in phlebovirus NPs cannot support a longitudinal assembly, and hence, their RNPs remain more loosely associated (Raymond et al., 2012) than in their plant-virus counterparts.
evidence: Inference from structural differences and reference to phlebovirus RNP structure.

claim: The structural homology suggests a horizontal gene transfer event between genera Potexvirus and Phlebovirus.
source: The current work provides data that suggest a horizontal gene transfer event between genera Potexvirus and Phlebovirus, or evolutionarily related forms.
evidence: Inference from the unexpected structural homology between evolutionarily distant viruses.

claim: Flexible filamentous viruses include economically important plant pathogens.
source: Flexible filamentous viruses include economically important plant pathogens.
evidence: General knowledge about flexible filamentous viruses.

claim: Flexible filamentous virus particles contain several hundred copies of a helically arrayed coat protein protecting a (+)ssRNA.
source: Their viral particles contain several hundred copies of a helically arrayed coat protein (CP) protecting a (+)ssRNA.
evidence: General knowledge about flexible filamentous virus structure.

claim: PepMV is a representative of the genus Potexvirus (family Alphaflexiviridae).
source: We describe here a structure at 3.9 Å resolution, from electron cryomicroscopy, of Pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), a representative of the genus Potexvirus (family Alphaflexiviridae).
evidence: Taxonomic classification of PepMV.

claim: The overall fold of PepMV CP resembles that of nucleoproteins from the genus Phlebovirus.
source: The overall fold of PepMV CP resembles that of nucleoproteins (NPs) from the genus Phlebovirus (family Bunyaviridae), a group of enveloped (-)ssRNA viruses.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: Phlebovirus is a group of enveloped (-)ssRNA viruses.
source: The overall fold of PepMV CP resembles that of nucleoproteins (NPs) from the genus Phlebovirus (family Bunyaviridae), a group of enveloped (-)ssRNA viruses.
evidence: General knowledge about phlebovirus characteristics.

claim: The main difference between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP is in their C-terminal extensions.
source: The main difference between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP is in their C-terminal extensions, which appear to determine the characteristics of the distinct multimeric assemblies – a flexuous, helical rod or a loose ribonucleoprotein.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis.

claim: C-terminal extensions determine the characteristics of distinct multimeric assemblies in potexvirus and phlebovirus.
source: The main difference between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP is in their C-terminal extensions, which appear to determine the characteristics of the distinct multimeric assemblies – a flexuous, helical rod or a loose ribonucleoprotein.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis of C-terminal regions and their roles in assembly.

claim: The homology between potexvirus CP and phlebovirus NP suggests gene transfer between eukaryotic (+) and (-)ssRNA viruses.
source: The homology suggests gene transfer between eukaryotic (+) and (-)ssRNA viruses.
evidence: Inference from the structural homology between evolutionarily distant virus groups.

claim: Flexible filamentous viruses have an enormous impact in agriculture.
source: Flexible filamentous viruses are ubiquitous plant pathogens that have an enormous impact in agriculture (Revers and Garcia, 2015).
evidence: Reference to review article on flexible filamentous viruses.

claim: Flexible filamentous virus particles are non-enveloped and flexible rod-shaped virions.
source: Their infective particles are non-enveloped and flexible rod-shaped virions (Kendall et al., 2008) and contain several hundreds of copies of a coat protein (CP) arranged in a helical fashion protecting a ssRNA of positive polarity, or (+)ssRNA (Kendall et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to review on flexible filamentous viruses.

claim: Flexible filamentous viruses are distributed in families Alphaflexiviridae, Betaflexiviridae, Closteroviridae, and Potyviridae.
source: They are distributed in families Alphaflexiviridae, Betaflexiviridae, Closteroviridae, and Potyviridae, which have different genomic organizations (particularly different between Potyviridae and the rest of the groups) and belong to different superfamilies, but it is thought that their CPs have strong evolutionary relationships (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to viral taxonomy and evolution.

claim: The CPs of flexible filamentous viruses are thought to have strong evolutionary relationships.
source: They are distributed in families Alphaflexiviridae, Betaflexiviridae, Closteroviridae, and Potyviridae, which have different genomic organizations (particularly different between Potyviridae and the rest of the groups) and belong to different superfamilies, but it is thought that their CPs have strong evolutionary relationships (Koonin et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to evolutionary analysis of viral proteins.

claim: Flexible plant virus filaments are 120-130 Å in diameter.
source: Structural studies of virions by X-ray fiber diffraction and cryoEM have indeed revealed a common architecture for flexible plant viruses. The filaments are 120-130 Å in diameter, and the CPs are arranged following helical symmetry with slightly less than 9 subunits per turn (Kendall et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to previous structural studies.

claim: CPs in flexible plant viruses are arranged following helical symmetry with slightly less than 9 subunits per turn.
source: Structural studies of virions by X-ray fiber diffraction and cryoEM have indeed revealed a common architecture for flexible plant viruses. The filaments are 120-130 Å in diameter, and the CPs are arranged following helical symmetry with slightly less than 9 subunits per turn (Kendall et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to previous structural studies.

claim: The overall helical arrangement is shared by SMV, PVX, PapMV, and NMV.
source: This overall arrangement is shared by Soybean mosaic virus (SMV) a potyvirus (from the family Potyviridae), and three different potexviruses (family Alphaflexiviridae), Potato virus X (PVX), Papaya mosaic virus (PapMV), and Narcissus mosaic virus (NMV) (Kendall et al., 2013, Yang et al., 2012, Kendall et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to previous structural studies of multiple viruses.

claim: The flexibility of virions has limited high-resolution structural studies.
source: The flexibility of the virions has limited high-resolution structural studies, and most of the previous data were at moderate resolution.
evidence: General observation about technical challenges in the field.

claim: The cryoEM structure of BaMV was determined at 5.6 Å.
source: Very recently, the cryoEM structure of Bamboo mosaic virus (BaMV), another potexvirus, was determined at 5.6 Å (DiMaio et al., 2015), and the CP was modeled based on the atomic structure of a truncated version of the CP from Papaya mosaic virus (PapMV CP) (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to recently published BaMV structure.

claim: N- and C-terminal extensions of the CP mediate viral polymerization and allow for the flexuous nature of virions.
source: The work revealed that N- and C-terminal extensions of the CP mediate viral polymerization and allow for the flexuous nature of the virions.
evidence: Reference to findings from BaMV structure study.

claim: PepMV has emerged recently and progressed from endemic to epidemic in tomato crops.
source: Pepino mosaic virus (PepMV) is another potexvirus which has emerged recently (Jones et al., 1980), progressing from endemic to epidemic in tomato crops causing severe economic losses worldwide (Hanssen and Thomma, 2010).
evidence: References to historical reports and epidemiological studies.

claim: PepMV causes severe economic losses worldwide in tomato crops.
source: Pepino mosaic virus (PepMV) is another potexvirus which has emerged recently (Jones et al., 1980), progressing from endemic to epidemic in tomato crops causing severe economic losses worldwide (Hanssen and Thomma, 2010).
evidence: Reference to epidemiological study.

claim: PepMV is transmitted by mechanical contact.
source: PepMV is transmitted by mechanical contact and virions contain a (+)ssRNA of about 6.4 kb (Aguilar et al., 2002).
evidence: Reference to PepMV characterization study.

claim: PepMV virions contain a (+)ssRNA of about 6.4 kb.
source: PepMV is transmitted by mechanical contact and virions contain a (+)ssRNA of about 6.4 kb (Aguilar et al., 2002).
evidence: Reference to PepMV genome characterization.

claim: PepMV CP is strictly required for cell-to-cell movement of the virus.
source: The PepMV CP is strictly required for cell-to-cell movement of the virus (Sempere et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to functional study of PepMV CP.

claim: The near-atomic 3D map allows for accurate modeling of the CP, the viral RNA, and their interaction.
